extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV viewers, critics, and researchers interested in political satire and Sacha Baron Cohen's work
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia-style article summarizing the television series Who Is America?, covering premise, characters, episodes, production/filming, marketing, reception, controversies, legal actions, ratings, and awards. Intended as a factual overview rather than a how-to or prescriptive guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise effectiveness / prosthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Baron Cohen found that increased fame made it more difficult to continue prank interviews without being recognized and therefore 'would need much more elaborate prosthetics' to hide his identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test disguises in real contexts (the page cites a February 2017 test interview where a beard, hat and glasses failed). Consult advanced makeup/prosthetics practitioners (mentions Rick Baker and Tony Gardner) and use realistic prosthetics and makeup as necessary to avoid recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden-camera / deception as method
rubrics_metrics.description: The show frequently used hidden cameras and deceptive booking practices to secure interviews and elicit unscripted reactions from public figures (e.g., segments filmed with hidden cameras and interviewees who were 'duped').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this method is integral to the show's approach but also raises ethical questions and can provoke strong negative responses from participants and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and legal risk from releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple interviewees claimed they were 'duped' and later pursued complaints or litigation; Roy Moore filed a $95 million suit alleging fraud and void consent. Courts ultimately dismissed Moore's claims citing release language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure robust, legally vetted release forms and anticipate challenges alleging fraudulent inducement; releases may preclude claims but litigation risk remains significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality / political relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The series 'explores the diverse individuals... across the political and cultural spectrum' and was explicitly inspired by post-2016 political events; critics noted its topicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and cultural relevance is a core evaluative dimension — being 'on point' can make segments powerful, but topicality alone doesn't guarantee success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shock / nihilistic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics described the show as having a 'nihilistic approach' and using shocking, unsettling material (Vanity Fair called parts 'unsettling' but funny once you get past the shock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shock can produce strong reactions and highlight issues, but risks alienating viewers or being characterized as gratuitous; balance intent and audience tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of comedic impact (hit-or-miss ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews characterized episodes as 'hit-and-miss' with some segments 'solid hits' and others 'weak, uninspired pieces'; audience tolerance depends on the ratio of successful to unsuccessful bits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate episodes by the proportion of segments that meaningfully land versus those that fall flat; editors and creators should curate episode composition accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception (aggregate scores and consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate critical metrics cited: Rotten Tomatoes 56% approval with average rating 6/10; Metacritic score 59/100 indicating 'mixed or average reviews'. The Rotten Tomatoes consensus: 'Fleetingly funny and all too relevant... nihilistic approach may not be the right way to say it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregator scores and critical consensus as a barometer of critical acceptance but complement with qualitative reviews for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewership and ratings performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiere viewership metrics: 327,000 live TV viewers plus 301,000 streaming/on-demand for a total of 628,000; noted demographic 18–49 rating of 0.1 and network-reported over a million viewers across platforms on premiere day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success via combined linear and streaming/platform metrics, demographic ratings, and signup impact (Showtime reported sign-up spikes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry recognition / awards and nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: The series received industry nominations (Golden Globe Best Actor nomination for Sacha Baron Cohen; DGA and multiple Primetime Emmy nominations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards and nominations are an evaluative dimension indicating professional/peer recognition beyond critics and ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing secrecy / promotional strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing relied on secrecy and teasers; early promos claimed NDAs prevented revealing title, premise or star, generating speculation before the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery and controlled information release can build pre-release buzz but may also create confusion or false speculation; coordinate teasers, NDAs, and publicity carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satirical props/gimmicks to elicit responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The show used fabricated devices and props (e.g., a farcical 'pedophile detector', a 'waterboard kit' signed by Dick Cheney) as part of satirical demonstrations and stunts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Props can be effective satirical tools to expose beliefs or behaviors, but they carry ethical and potential legal implications and may attract controversy or additional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential real-world political and social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments led to tangible consequences for participants (e.g., Jason Spencer's televised behavior prompted criticism and his subsequent resignation) and broader public debate about deception in journalism/entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and anticipate downstream effects on subjects' careers and public discourse when producing provocative satire; consider potential harm and public interest justification.
